title: How did Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles win Sight and Sound's greatest film of all time award?

commenti.body:
I think what might be part of the reason is, Jeanne Dielman made the list in 2012 as well, but on a lower spot. This upped viewership, since many (especially those who vote on the list) watch every film on the Sight & Sound list, leading them to discover the film, thus opening the doors for the list to climb the charts.

Another part of it may be the fact that the BFI expanded voters this year to a lot more women critics and filmmakers, who are arguably more versed in classic films from women filmmakers, thus having seen Jeanne Dielman.

Also, in general, I think Jeanne Dielman may be more obscure among more mainstream film watchers, but within more serious film fabs it’s a lot more widely known (especially since it’s had a Criterion release for years now). 

Just my two cents.

I am very confused by this too? Look, I am not denying that Jeanne Dielman is a great film and people are glad that it is receiving recognition.

It is just that, if you are a real film snob, nobody would know what Jeanne Dielman is and probably wouldn't have the time and day to watch it. and if you really delved into the plot of Jeanne Dielman, it is about a housewife who does chores. Very...Very Mundanely. compare that to Vertigo and Citizen Kane. with Vertigo essentially being the peak of Hitchcock and being the ultimate of what Hitchcock as done and Citizen Kane, in which Orson Welles pretty much revolutionized and change the game in Hollywood.

Jeanne Dielman is a film made in Belgium that unless you're a film snob, you probably haven't heard of it. Hell when I saw the poll, I was like, "What The Hell Of Jeanne Dielman"?

It’s because most critics were pressured by their employers (since the votes are public) to vote for at least one film with a female director. Since there aren’t that many in the canon, everyone is voting for the same three films. Whereas, there are a lot of critics that don’t put Citizen Kane or Vertigo in their top 10.

>such an obscure movie

I'll let others explain the film's merits better but I'd like to point out how incredibly condescending it can be to call any film you personally never watched/heard about as 'obscure'.

I had a discussion sometime ago with a so-called film buff friend who referred to anything either made before 1990 or made outside of the US as 'obscure' and 'oh this film's great, sad I'm probably the only one who's seen it'. Stuff like Satoshi Kon's anime films or even The Seventh Seal were considered "obscure" by this person.

This made me feel an ick because it was almost as if enjoying films that are outside of an established cannon was somehow "silly" since these are obscure and no one has seen them.

And then, I go back to the more succint argument: less than 5% of all film production in history would be considered "popular" in such strict therms. The fact that no one in your neighborhood has seen Jeanne Dielman doesn't make it an "obscure" film.

There is such a thing as "niche", of course, in that pieces of art have their own followings and admirers without it being necessarily mainstream, and without it being 'obscure', as that word would mean it would be difficult to find ways to watch it at all.

And Chantal Akerman is a perfectly known filmmaker to anyone who doesn't let this 'obscureness' blur their exploration of film. Especially people who are interested in documentary and experimental film.

​

>Belgian film made nearly fifty years ago

Citizen Kane was released eighty years ago, and Vertigo, sixty-five. I don't see the point in commenting their ages.

​

>over movies everyone has seen

That would imply maybe only films as famous as 'Avengers: Endgame' should be in it? Citizen Kane and Vertigo are also niche, in that not everyone watches classic cinema, let alone if it's produced outside their home countries.

It's only when it's non-US produced that it becomes "obscure". I just feel like rolling my eyes.

This movie has been famous among film critics and scholars since it came out. Criterion released it on DVD in 2009. I watched it when I was in school years before that. And that is who votes for this poll. Part of its big jump is that the voter pool was expanded between the last poll and this one but it was very well seen among the crowd who selects the list before that.

It’s not as if Citizens Kane was some super popular film among the general public always either. It has had decades to grow into the essential classic it is now seen as. As has Vertigo; that’s a product of film scholars boosting more than anything I think. But their boosting has been longer and thus gone more mainstream (plus their makers are more famous) so you’ve heard of them. Also they’re in English.
The people who vote in this poll are professionals. It’s their job to know more than you and me. But the good thing is their job is also to help us learn about this stuff which they’ve done.

This couldn't be more wrong. Jeanne Dielman has been critically acclaimed for decades. It was 19th on The Village Voice's Greatest Films of the 20th Century and has continued to gain respect.

And Chantal Akerrman is a brilliant, brilliant filmmaker regardless of her gender, but that gender provides a fantastic POV.

Sight & Sounds contributors are familiar with many, many films that even casual cinephiles aren't--in fact, S&S is my go-to for expanding my film vocabulary. While I might not always agree with their rankings (and in this case I'd put Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce in my top 10-15, not #1), I appreciate the thought and intelligence that their contributors bring to this rankings.
In addition to the other comments, it’s my understanding that the way the voting and scoring system works for S&S, small changes in votes can lead to significant moves up or down the ranks

The fact that Jeanne Dielman is actually much *younger* than Citizen Kane and Vertigo is one reason why it is possible for it to make a big jump (over a 10 year period). Its perceived greatness is still being determined.

To fill a quota basically. This video does a good job of explaining why:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A1TGqXkZSno&ab\_channel=Moviewise](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A1TGqXkZSno&ab_channel=Moviewise)

I think it's not really much different than Shawshank Redemption getting the highest marks because of an internal IMDb feud between fans of the Godfather and The Dark Knight.

I think there are 'chip on the shoulder' critics who are voting for this particular film because it not a masculine driven narrative.

There, of course, people who like the film intrinsically.

Then I think there are critics who wouldn't put Jeanne at the very top of their " best of" lists but create hype just by mentioning it.


So I do think it's kind of a bunch of different factors, and not just basic virtue signaling.

One *potential* part of the explanation is that all voting systems are susceptible to "strategic" voting, but the Sight and Sound voting system is especially susceptible to it. (The most obvious example of this is when a director has several acclaimed movies, there is a very strong incentive for that director's fans to "fall in line" behind a single film even if a voter doesn't actually believe that film to be their best. On the flip side, those who do not fall in line end up "splitting" the vote.)

It's entirely possible that a some voters intentionally overrated Jeanne Dielman on their ballots because they felt that it was underrated on the previous Sight and Sound poll, leading to an overcorrection. (Though we'll have to wait 10 years to see if this theory has any merit.)

Is that the plot? Are you sure? 

Spoiler- it’s not.

I think it’s partly due to voters assuming everyone else is going to be voting citizen kane, vertigo etc. and so go for a more interesting pick which then leads everyone to do that and crown a shock winner

I don’t think it’s “obscure”, I’ve known about it for 20 years or more. But it did take me until it got the top spot to watch it. I won’t be doing that again. 

But how did it get the top spot? Being on peoples lists, obviously.

"Was their lobbying done ala the Oscars?"

Yes lots of critics championed this film over others as what should be the top of the list. The other key factor was expanding the voting pool to more diverse persons. The elevation of Jeanne Dielman was a direct result of these two factors. You're absolutely right that this is a more obscure idiosyncratic film that really is an odd choice to be at the top of the list.

Its methodology of counting each submitted top 10 (unranked) list might not be the best way to determine the so-called "best movie of all time".   As long as JD appears on more lists than others, it will be ranked as #1.    Even when more writers think Citizen Kane is the greatest, and JD is the 10th best, as long as JD gets in one more list, it still wins out.  That doesn't sound like a good way to determine the best of all time.  But Sight & Sound has a long tradition of polling, aside from a few tweaks, it has done so the same way.  I just don't take those "Best of All Time" polls seriously.  I do find the poll results pretty cool, especially looking back on its history, and how one film moves up and others fade into obscurity.

>This made me feel an ick because it was almost as if enjoying films that are outside of an established cannon was somehow "silly" since these are obscure and no one has seen them.

Did this "so-called film buff friend" make fun of you for enjoying older, non-English films? Because it's not clear why you take "obscure" as an insult when it's just describing that the average American hasn't seen a lot of non-English movies made from three decades ago and before.

Let's go ask 100 random people about movies that fit this definition and I think we'd be more than validated in calling them obscure.

>'obscure', as that word would mean it would be difficult to find ways to watch it at all.

Can I go to my local big box store and walk out with a Blu-ray of Jeanne Dielman? Is it on Netflix? Does it get annual reruns at my local multiplex? No? Why do you get heated that someone thinks Jeanne Dielman is obscure, but then set up and prove your own definition of obscure? And again, why is being obscure an insult to you?

>That would imply maybe only films as famous as 'Avengers: Endgame' should be in it? Citizen Kane and Vertigo are also niche, in that not everyone watches classic cinema, let alone if it's produced outside their home countries.

Oh please. Citizen Kane and Vertigo are more famous and much more influential than Jeanne Dielman, and by a huge margin. You can blame sexism, but let's be honest Jeanne Dielman is a lot less accessible to 99% of audiences who are going to get bored to tears even if the statement is radical.

While mainstream popularity may not be a direct reflection of a movie's quality, there also needs to be some observable cultural impact to really consider a piece of cinema to be amongst the greatest of all time when discussing a poll as prolific as Sight & Sound. Cinema, like theater before it, is an art for the masses. Frankly I don't think that Chantal Akerman herself would have considered Jeanne Dielman to be the greatest of all time. It's clearly niche in its intent—and that's fine.

It sounds like you're just mad that American films are the most consistently popular around the world and that your circle of sophisticated film fans aren't reflective of most people's tastes.
I have better stuff to do with my time than answering this shit. What an incredibly narrow-minded point of view for a sub such as truefilm.

I hate to sound like the snobby arthouse cinephile who tell people they don't know anything about the art, so just know that this isnt an attack on your cinema knowledge or anything, but: Jeanne Dielman was already a classic and widely acclaimed in plenty of circles way before the 2022 S&S poll, you just didn't realise it. It was hailed as a masterpiece by plenty of critics, highly regarded filmmakers like Van Sant cited it as a direct inspiration for their work, and any scholar that took the tiniest interest into feminist and/or queer cinema history knows Ackerman and her work. Hell, it was already pretty high on the 2012 S&S list, higher than films like the 400 Blows or La Dolce Vita! So it's not a random film that came out of nowhere, it was already a cult classic that found a way to grow enough in popularity to win the poll. I think that what made it jump to the top is because:


- the S&S poll being an institution, I assume people watch/rewatch the stuff that ended high between polls. It benefits films like Jeanne Dielman that get "discovered" by some people through it, rather than Vertigo that everyone already knows.

- the S&S poll extended his voter pool to be more diverse. It shook a lot of things up in the rankings overall, including films directed by women to be gaining positions compared to the 2012 poll in general. 

- the Belgian Cinematek did a lot of work to preserve, share and promote Ackerman's work in the past decade. That includes the creation of the Ackerman Fondation and the restoration of plenty of her films. That played a big part in cementing her legacy.
